title: A hymn in Asa
hookLine: the hymn that opens Asa asks where the door is

lines: ONE SONG, MORE THAN ONE ROOM.
cards: Some songs you meet in more than one room. You hear one at a wedding, then in a car, then hummed by someone at the sink, and each time it sounds a little different. The Guru Granth Sahib has a hymn like that.
A Sikh who has prayed the Japji in the morning has said it. A Sikh who has prayed the Rehras in the evening has said it.
And open the Granth to the first page of Raga Asa, and there it is again, standing at the door of the whole section.

teach.b: It's called So Dar, from its first words, that door.
Guru Nanak opens with a question, given here in plain English: what is that door, what is that house, where you sit and take care of everything?
A few days ago, with the string instruments, you heard part of the answer from the Japji: instruments and players beyond counting. Here it goes on.
The winds sing, the waters sing, fire sings. The keepers of what's right and wrong sing. The truthful, the contented, the brave.
And the hymn admits its list will never be finished: many others sing, it says, whom Nanak can't even call to mind. Notice what Guru Nanak doesn't do. He never gives the door an address.
No hill, no temple. Then listen to how the hymn ends, the part a first hearing rushes past.
That One, it says, is the King, the King over kings, and Nanak lives within that will. The question was where. The answer, in the end, is how: stand inside the will, and you're already at the door.
That's why it opens Asa so well.

At dawn, the raga's first hymn asks where God lives and answers with a way to live the day. Asa holds more as you go on: the Patti, a hymn built on the letters of a child's writing board, and the dawn ballad itself.
But the way into the section is a door, a song, and a will to live inside.

how: Sikhs meet So Dar in daily prayer: a version of it is part of the Japji, and it is sung or recited as part of the Rehras in the evening. In kirtan it is also sung as a shabad of Raga Asa.

games.q: what does “a hymn in asa” mean?
o: a wedding hymn sung at the door of the home
a hymn naming the gurdwara where God lives
So Dar, the hymn at the door of Raga Asa

games.q: what's inside the hymn — tap the pairs.
p: where do you sit and care for all?
a hymn on a child's writing board

s: So Dar gives God's house an address
it never names a place; it answers with all creation singing.
a version of So Dar is also in the Japji and the Rehras
the same hymn is met in morning prayer, evening prayer, and at the start of Asa.
the hymn says its list of singers is complete
it says there are more singers than anyone could name.

games.q: you're asked: where is God's house? what does Guru Nanak's hymn do?
o: lists the voices singing at the door.
games.why: So Dar asks what that door and house are, then answers with winds, waters, fire, seekers and more, all singing there, too many to name.

practice: Close your eyes if that's comfortable and start with the nearest sound, your breath, a fridge humming, traffic, wind, letting each one count as a voice in that crowd at the door.

Then reach a little farther for the next sound, and the next, letting each join in without naming it for long. If you pray, say Waheguru under your breath, adding one more voice; if you don't, simply keep listening outward.

wordCard.voice: A hymn in Asa. So Dar, that door, the hymn that opens Raga Asa, which hears all creation singing where God sits. Today's word.

orig.note: so dar, that door: the opening words of the hymn that begins Raga Asa.

carryVoice: Your line: the dawn raga. The question was where, and the answer was how: within that will. Go gently.

sources.ref: So Dar in the Rehras, Ang 8–9
